definition: It is the poet's right to ignore rules and conventions generally observed by users of the language.
Refers to the ways in which certain aspects of a text can be made to stand out or appear prominent through forms of textual patterning.
Extra regular use of a linguistic feature; it helps readers perceive semantic relations between words.
Extra irregularity that works by disrupting or departing from readers' expectations.
Is achieved through neologism, which is the invention of new words.
The invention of new words in which a poet may exceed the normal resources of the language.
New words made up for a single occasion.
Adapting an item to a new grammatical function without changing its form.
Deviating from the syntactic constraints, such as putting the adjective after the noun.
A matter of typography, layout, punctuation, and spelling that adopt modes of layout peculiar to poetry.
Emerges from meaning relations which are logically inconsistent or paradoxical, such as metaphor.
The linguistic means by which sentences are woven together to make texts.
Cases where the content words of a passage can be seen to 'naturally' go together.
Covers cases where we use a grammatical word in one sentence in association with a word in a separate sentence.
Material is left out since its repetition or near-repetition is felt to be unnecessary.
Refers to the use of certain words or phrases to clarify the semantic or logical relationship of information.
The cover term for the ways available to a speaker for expressing 'opinion or attitude'.
Sentences which assert something to be a general truth, typically timelessly true.
A one-sentence summary of what transpired in a narrative.
Sentences describing the participants, the time and place of events in a story.
Sentences in which the all-important and ordered events of the narrative are reported.
Material which highlights how a story is interesting or relevant to the listener.
The narrative's answer to the question: 'So what finally happened?'
A bridge back to the teller-addressee present, often providing a lesson learned.
Transition points in conversation at which other speakers are drawn to respond and react.
Your wish to be liked by others and have your interests approved of.
Your wish not to be coerced or forced into things; the desire to be free from imposition.
Avoiding any explicit mention of the goods or services requested, essentially dropping a hint.
Drawing explicit attention to and containing a direct semantic link with the service requested.
Actions performed via utterances, such as promising, threatening, or requesting.
The basic assumption that speakers normally intend to accomplish purposeful and effective communication.
The rule to make your contribution one that is true and not say things that are false.
The rule to make your contribution as informative as is required—not too much or too little.
The rule to say things that are relevant in the context.
The rule to be clear and avoid unnecessary obscurity or ambiguity.
Occurs where the norm is the background of the remainder of the poem itself.
Occurs where the deviation is measured against a norm that lies outside the limits of the poem.
The function or communicative force behind an utterance (what is intended).
The effect or result that an utterance has on the listener.
When there is a direct relationship between a linguistic structure and a function.
When there is an indirect relationship between a linguistic structure and a function.
